query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the HVAF-i7 deposition by increasing the in-flight particle velocity—achieved by reducing the spray distance to approximately 300–350 mm—will overcome the thickness limitation of FeCoNiCrAl bond coats while maintaining low in-spray oxidation and adhesion.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a feedstock size of 15–45 μm, known to produce high-quality coatings under HVAF-M3 conditions.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 torch parameters to increase particle velocity by reducing the nozzle-to-substrate spray distance to around 300–350 mm.
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch on substrates (including those with inner diameters as small as 120 mm) under conditions equivalent to those used with the HVAF-M3 system, with identical powder feedstock.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic impact energy promotes better particle deformation and bonding, leading to a denser, thicker deposit with controlled oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Higher in-flight particle velocity increases the kinetic energy upon impact, improving flattening and inter-particle bonding while reducing the in-flight residence time, which minimizes oxidation. This is analogous to the slight deposition efficiency gain observed for MCrAlY bond coats at higher velocity and optimum spray distances.
generation.predicted_outcome: The increased particle velocity will yield a significantly thicker and adherent bond coat compared to the baseline HVAF-i7 conditions, with minimal as-sprayed oxidation and sustained high-temperature durability.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with the standard HVAF-i7 operating parameters using 15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl powder, which result in acceptable coating quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under deposition conditions similar to those used in HVAF-M3 studies (i.e., optimal spray distances around 300–350 mm) and on substrates with internal diameters ∼120 mm. However, excessive increase in particle velocity could induce overheating or phase instabilities, which may counteract the beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in deposition thickness and potential impacts on coating microstructure (e.g., residual stresses or phase transformation due to altered thermal histories) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study where FeCoNiCrAl coatings are deposited using the HVAF-i7 torch with two sets of parameters. Group A uses standard HVAF-i7 conditions and spray distances, while Group B employs increased particle velocity by reducing the spray distance to approximately 300–350 mm. Both groups will use the same 15–45 μm feedstock and be applied to substrates with 120 mm internal diameter.
measurements: Oxide content and phase distribution (EDS/XRD analyses)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Group B does not show a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (e.g., improvement >10% over Group A) without a concurrent deterioration in oxidation resistance or adhesion properties, then the hypothesis that increasing particle velocity by reducing spray distance overcomes the thickness limitation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

cited_evidence.text: The intermetallic compounds of the Ti–Al system are known not to pest []. Aluminium rich TiAl, and the TiAl2 and TiAl3 aluminides can form alumina scales but Al poor TiAl and Ti3Al form titania rich scales and oxidise at much higher rates []. For example, when TiAl with 50 at.% Al was oxidised in air at 950, 1100 and 1200 °C, at the two higher temperatures TiO2 scale formed and there was internal oxidation. Parabolic oxidation kinetics were followed at the low temperature where the oxidation was independent of specimen preparation and fabrication method []. Furthermore, the alloying of TiAl with Nb promoted the formation of continuous alumina scale on TiAl (50 at.% Al) at 950 °C independent of surface preparation or exposure environment (air or O2) but the alloying with Hf had a minimal effect []. The alloying of TiAl with Si improved oxidation resistance []. For Al poor TiAl it is known that the addition of 4 to 12 at.% Nb in Ti–48Al increased oxidation resistance at 850 °C and that the alloys developed continuous bands of dense alumina beneath titania rich surface layer that formed during the early stages of oxidation [].
